Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-20 16:00 UTC

Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (Oceanic Head of ML Infra), Ava Rodriguez (Platform Eng), Tom Hsu (SRE)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, sorry for the slight delay, we had a calendar glitch. I'm Maya from Redwood, with Liam our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:18] Sanjay Patel: Good, thanks Maya. We are excited to get into the nitty gritty today. Our main ask is to validate we won't drop SLA during marketing bursts which are, uh, pretty spiky.
[00:30] Liam Ortega: Great — that's exactly what we wanted to cover. We'll walk through queueing models, how Redwood's autoscaler behaves under Poisson-like bursts, KV cache warmup, and the reserve/prewarm pool options.
[01:05] Ava Rodriguez: Quick note — we plan to run the private deployment in our VPC with HSM-backed KMS. We need to know if prewarmed GPUs require any special network egress or KMS calls that could be blocked by our rules.
[01:25] Liam Ortega: Good call — prewarmed pools just sit behind the private control plane. KMS calls only happen during model startup if you're using encrypted model weights, otherwise runtime calls are minimal. But we will detail the flow in the checklist.
[02:10] Tom Hsu: Also curious about graceful degradation — if we hit a burst beyond capacity, do requests queue or do we fail fast and fallback to a smaller model variant?
[02:30] Liam Ortega: By policy. You can set routing rules: prefer low latency up to X qps, overflow to a cheaper quantized variant, or return a 429. Many customers use an ordered fallback: reserve pool -> dedicated spot -> quantized fallback.
[03:05] Sanjay Patel: We're worried about tail latencies. Our SLO is p99 under 350ms for single-turn generations; some longer-context requests are allowed more time. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[03:35] Liam Ortega: Guarantees depend on reserved capacity and prewarmed GPUs. If you commit to a pool sized for peak QPS and use KV prefix caching, you can hit p99 targets. Otherwise autoscaler targets throughput and may introduce a small startup latency for scale-outs — typically seconds, not tens of seconds, but depends on model and quantization.
[04:12] Maya Chen: To be explicit: for p99 350ms we usually recommend a combination: reserved baseline capacity sized to handle median+tail buffer (approx 1.5x median), plus a small burst reserve and a fast quantized variant for fallback. We'll send a sizing worksheet.
[05:00] Liam Ortega: Let's sketch the queueing model we often use — think M/M/c with bursty arrivals approximated by a compound Poisson; in practice we simulate using the real traffic trace. If arrivals exceed warm capacity, requests either queue (bounded queue) or are routed to fallback.
[05:30] Sanjay Patel: Can you walk through KV cache behavior during a burst? We rely heavily on prefix cache for conversational state.
[05:52] Liam Ortega: Sure. Two main behaviors: "hot prefix" caching for recent tokens and KV cache reuse when the same conversation continues. For burst events where many new conversations start, there's a cold-start penalty as KV must be allocated and warmed.
[06:20] Tom Hsu: How big is that cold-start penalty for our LLMs? We run a 32k-context model with quantized weights (4-bit).
[06:35] Liam Ortega: With quantization we see slightly faster memory traffic but warmup allocation still costs time — typically 200-600ms per model instantiation depending on sequence length and kernel compile hit rate. If you prewarmed pool you can avoid that.
[07:10] Ava Rodriguez: Is continuous batching compatible with prewarmed instances? We can't block prewarming if batching increases latency.
[07:30] Liam Ortega: Yes, prewarmed instances accept batching. Continuous batching is workload-aware — it will batch requests up to your configured latency SLO. You can tune batch size and batch latency threshold per route.
[08:30] Sanjay Patel: We had a bad incident where scaling caused a thundering herd — many instances tried to warm and hit our internal model registry causing spikes in registry calls. Anything to prevent that?
[08:50] Liam Ortega: We recommend staggered prewarm and jittered backoff; Redwood's orchestrator staggers startups by default to avoid registry storms. Also you can cache images/models in a local registry mirror in your VPC to reduce central hits.
[09:30] Maya Chen: We'll put a runbook in the playbook on staggered warmups and registry mirroring.
[10:15] Liam Ortega: Also about autoscale policies — we support a few modes: reactive (cpu/gpu util), request-based (qps/latency), and predictive (traffic model-based). Predictive uses your historical trace to pre-provision for expected bursts.
[12:30] Sanjay Patel: Can predictive handle sudden marketing bursts timed to an external event? Our historical traces are sparse for that pattern.
[12:51] Liam Ortega: If you can provide a synthetic marketing-burst trace, we can inject it into the predictor to prewarm. For unknown bursts, a hybrid policy (small reserve + aggressive predictive assigment) tends to work best.
[15:05] Tom Hsu: Let's talk reserved GPU sizing — how to calculate reserved baseline for steady-state vs bursts?
[15:30] Liam Ortega: Start with median throughput and median token/sec per request. Multiply to get required sustained token throughput, then factor in batching gains and KV cache hit rate. Then add a tail buffer: for example if median is 100 qps, p95 is 220 qps, reserve for 220 qps and leave autoscaler to handle beyond that. We usually recommend 1.2-1.8x median depending on cost tolerance.
[16:20] Sanjay Patel: How does quantization impact throughput and tail latency? Any surprises for 4-bit run?
[16:42] Liam Ortega: Quantization reduces memory bandwidth and often increases throughput, but may slightly increase per-token compute depending on kernel implementation. Also accuracy tradeoffs matter; many customers use quantized fallback for burst overflow but keep FP16 for baseline.
[18:00] Ava Rodriguez: For on-prem air-gapped environments, are there additional warmup considerations?
[18:22] Liam Ortega: Yes: image and model caches must be seeded manually; no external kernel downloads at runtime. Prewarm is even more important on-prem since network pulls are slow or blocked. We provide an offline package for the runtime.
[19:05] Maya Chen: Quick aside — some of the terminology in the transcript may show "K V cache" or "KVC ash" in automated text, ignore those typos — it's KV cache.
[20:15] Sanjay Patel: For the pilot, we want to simulate our peak: 3x baseline sustained for 30 minutes with microbursts of 50% above peak every 2 minutes. Can Redwood run that?
[20:35] Liam Ortega: Yes. We'll run a 48-hour pilot that includes that synthetic pattern, plus a failover drill where we intentionally reduce reserved pool by 40% and observe routing/fallback behavior.
[21:05] Tom Hsu: What metrics will you capture? We need p50/p95/p99 latencies, tail queue length, instance startup times, KV cache hit rate, and token cost breakdown.
[21:25] Liam Ortega: All of those. We'll provide a dashboard link and CSV export. We'll also include per-route tracing to see which requests hit the quantized fallback.
[22:40] Ava Rodriguez: About security: can the prewarm process access external key services? We have strict egress controls.
[23:00] Liam Ortega: Prewarm does not require external egress if you seed model artifacts and images. KMS calls only if you use cloud KMS for decrypting model weights at startup. The private package supports HSM integration but we'll need to confirm exact calls for your HSM vendor.
[24:10] Sanjay Patel: Any guidance on queue sizes? We don't want unbounded queues.
[24:32] Liam Ortega: We recommend bounded queues sized to expected backlog (e.g., 2-5x avg in-flight). If queue gets near capacity, older requests can be canceled or rerouted. Also you can set per-customer or per-route concurrency caps.
[25:20] Maya Chen: Let's run a short scenario — assume baseline reserved capacity for 200 qps, typical request cost 150 tokens average, batch multiplier 1.8x, KV hit rate 70%. How do we estimate the headroom?
[26:00] Liam Ortega: You'd estimate sustained token throughput: 200 * 150 = 30k tokens/sec. With batching 1.8x effective, you need less raw GPUs. But tail events reduce effective batching, so factor in lower batching during spikes. We'll put a sizing sheet with formulas.
[28:00] Sanjay Patel: For failover drills, what's the recommended schedule and who should be on-call?
[28:20] Maya Chen: We recommend a runbook war-game: staging drill first, then production with a narrow blast radius (10% traffic), then a full-scale drill. On-call should include SRE, platform, and Redwood SE for the first run.
[30:05] Tom Hsu: Any gotchas with observability latency? We can't have dashboards lagging by minutes.
[30:30] Liam Ortega: Our metrics pipeline supports near-real-time (sub-10s) for critical SLO metrics. Logs and detailed traces may be slightly delayed but you get immediate p99/p95 windows.
[32:10] Ava Rodriguez: Is there an overhead for enabling per-token cost breakdown at token-level?
[32:30] Liam Ortega: Minimal. We sample token-level accounting on a route-by-route basis to avoid excessive ingestion. You can enable full accounting for high-cost routes.
[35:30] Sanjay Patel: About prewarming: how many prewarmed instances do we need per reserved GPU?
[35:50] Liam Ortega: Prewarmed instances are 1:1 with reserved slots usually. You can set a ratio if you accept some cold starts. The orchestration can keep X instances hot per pool.
[37:10] Maya Chen: We'll attach a suggested mapping in the spreadsheet based on your trace.
[38:45] Liam Ortega: One more thing — progressive rollouts: Redwood supports canary traffic steering so you can test quantized variants on 1-2% traffic before enabling as fallback. This helps catch quality regressions.
[40:00] Sanjay Patel: Good. For compliance we need audit logs of model version rollout and KMS access.
[40:20] Liam Ortega: Audit logs are built-in for Private deployments and include model rollouts, who triggered it, and KMS request metadata. We'll share the SOC2 checklist.
[42:00] Tom Hsu: If we decide to use on-prem isolated hardware, any advice for kernel selection and quantization?
[42:22] Liam Ortega: We will run a quick kernel compatibility test against your GPUs. For quantization we prefer per-channel symmetric quantization for memory-constrained setups; we'll surface recommended quant config per model.
[44:00] Ava Rodriguez: Ok, let's define the concrete pilot scope now: 48-hour dedicated pool, synthetic marketing trace included, one failover drill mid-run, and deliver dashboards + CSVs.
[44:20] Maya Chen: Agreed. We'll provision a test pool and share credentials for your team to observe.
[45:00] Sanjay Patel: One last question — what's the expected cost delta if we maintain 1.5x reserved vs 2.0x? Ballpark.
[45:25] Liam Ortega: Roughly linear for reserved GPU charges; 2.0x will be ~33% more than 1.5x on reserved spend but may reduce autoscale egress charges. We'll put a cost simulation in the sheet.
[46:30] Maya Chen: Ok let's recap next steps — Maya will share the bench sheet, Liam shares configs, Oceanic provides traces, Redwood runs the pilot and schedules a failover war-game.
[47:05] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Thanks — appreciate the clear runbook.
[47:20] Tom Hsu: Thanks team.
[47:40] Maya Chen: We'll follow up with calendar invites for the run and the drill.
[48:00] End of call (wrap and small chitchat omitted)
